summary: This informational memo describes how to invoke transcoding services in SIP using third-party call control. This meets the requirements for supporting deaf, hard of hearing and speech-impaired users.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4117 shows how a SIP call can be routed through a machine that converts between media types, so that for example a deaf user working in text can take part in a call with someone speaking audio. The other end invites the transcoder, the two sides of the call are set up as separate sessions, and the memo gives the exact message sequence for several arrangements.

subtitle: How a SIP call gets a transcoding service put in the middle of it, so both ends can still talk.

tldr.problem: Two SIP endpoints that cannot understand each other, for example one that only speaks text and one that only speaks audio, need a transcoding service, and the signalling to bring it in had not been worked out.
tldr.mechanism: The memo shows the third party call control model in use: the transcoder is identified by a URI, one endpoint invites it, and the two sessions it sets up are negotiated with SDP, in several different arrangements.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational memo that gives message flows rather than a new protocol, and it notes that the transcoder has to see the media in the clear, so it behaves as a man in the middle by definition.

facts.label: Media streams in the callee example

today: RFC 4117 is an Informational memo published in June 2005, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It gives the message flows for invoking a transcoding service with third party call control, building on the best current practices for 3pcc in RFC 3725.

sections.title: Why Transcoding Needs Its Own Signalling
sections.content:
The framework for transcoding with SIP describes how two SIP user agents can discover incompatibilities that prevent them from establishing a session, for example a lack of support for a common codec or a common media type. When such incompatibilities are found, the user agents need to invoke transcoding services to successfully establish the session. Third party call control, or 3pcc, is one way to perform such invocation.

The memo is careful about the limits of its own scope. It describes how to invoke transcoding services, not how the transcoding itself works: the way the transcoder manipulates and manages the contents of the media streams is service specific. All the call flows use SDP, and the same call flows could be used with another session description protocol that provides similar capabilities.
sections.plainLanguage: When two programs cannot understand each other's media, something has to sit between them and translate. The translation itself is not standardized, and this memo does not standardize it. What it standardizes is the set of messages that put the translator in place.

sections.title: The General Model
sections.content:
In the 3pcc model for transcoding invocation, a transcoding server that provides a particular transcoding service, for example speech-to-text, is identified by a URI. A user agent that wishes to invoke that service sends an INVITE request to that URI, establishing a number of media streams.

Given two user agents, A and B, and a transcoding server T, the invocation of a transcoding service consists of establishing two sessions, A-T and T-B. How these sessions are established depends on which party, the caller A or the callee B, invokes the transcoding service. The memo follows a general principle in all its flows: a 200 OK response from the transcoding service has to be received before contacting the callee, which tries to ensure that the transcoding service will be available when the callee accepts the session.

The memo also notes a limit of the approach. The transcoding service does not know the exact type of transcoding it will be performing until the callee accepts the session, so there is always a chance of failing to provide transcoding services after the callee has accepted. A system with more stringent requirements could use preconditions to avoid this, in which case the callee is not alerted until everything is ready for the session.

The flows use a naming convention for the session descriptions. SDP A is a session description generated by A, containing among other things the transport address or addresses, an IP address and a port number, where A wants to receive media for each particular stream. SDP B is the same from B. SDP A+B is a session description that contains the addresses where A wants to receive media and the addresses where B wants to receive media. SDP TA is a session description generated by T and intended for A, containing the addresses where T wants to receive media from A, and SDP TB is the same for B. SDP TA+TB is generated by T and contains the addresses where T wants to receive media from A and from B.
sections.plainLanguage: The transcoder is just another server with an address of its own, and it is added to the call by being invited. Two sessions then exist where there was one. The rule the memo keeps is that the transcoder must say yes before the other party is contacted, so that the call does not fall apart after it has been accepted.

sections.title: The Callee Invokes the Transcoder
sections.content:
In this scenario B receives an INVITE from A and decides to introduce T into the session. In the example, A can both hear and speak, and B is a deaf user with a speech impairment. A proposes to establish a session that consists of an audio stream. B wants to send and receive only text, so it invokes a transcoding service T that will perform both speech-to-text and text-to-speech conversions.

The flow is as follows. A sends an INVITE with SDP A, offering one audio stream at A's own address. B, instead of answering A directly, sends an INVITE with SDP A+B to the transcoder, describing both the audio stream at A and a text stream at B. The transcoder answers with 200 OK and SDP TA+TB, giving the addresses it will use for both directions, and B acknowledges. The transcoder then sends 200 OK with SDP TA back to A, and A acknowledges.

At that point four media streams have been established, that is two bi-directional streams: audio from A to T.example.com on port 30000, text from T to B.example.com on port 40000, text from B to T.example.com on port 30002, and audio from T to A.example.com on port 20000. When either A or B decides to terminate the session, it sends a BYE indicating that the session is over.

If the first INVITE received by B is empty, that is it carries no session description, the call flow is slightly different. B may have different reasons for invoking T before knowing A's session description: B may want to hide its lack of native capabilities, and therefore wants to return a session description with all the codecs that B supports, plus all the codecs that T supports, or T may provide recording services besides transcoding and B wants T to record the conversation whether or not transcoding is needed. In this case B still does not have SDP A when it sends INVITE to T, so it cannot pass that information on. When B finally receives SDP A, it has to send it to T, which means B sends an empty INVITE to T and gets a 200 OK with SDP TA+TB. In general that SDP TA+TB can be different from the one sent earlier, which is why B has to send the updated SDP TA to A, A sends a possibly updated SDP A back, and B sends that to T. On the other hand, if T happens to return the same SDP TA+TB, B can skip three of those messages. Implementors of transcoding services are therefore encouraged to return the same session description in the second answer as in the first in this type of scenario.
sections.plainLanguage: The deaf user, on receiving the call, invites the transcoder instead of answering the caller. The transcoder tells both sides where to send their media, and after that the call runs as two separate sessions with the translator in the middle. If the caller did not say what it could do, the description has to be passed along afterwards, and the transcoder is asked twice.

sections.title: Other Ways of Invoking and of Receiving the Original Stream
sections.content:
Caller's invocation. In this scenario A wishes to establish a session with B using a transcoding service, and uses 3pcc to set up the session between T and B. The flow provided is slightly different from the ones in the 3pcc best current practices, because in that document the controller establishes a session between two user agents, which are the ones deciding the characteristics of the streams. Here, A wants to establish a session between T and B, but A wants to decide how many and which types of streams are established. That is why A sends its session description in the first INVITE to T, as opposed to the media-less initial INVITE recommended there. The memo does not give the session descriptions for this flow, since they are very similar to those in the earlier figure, and notes that if T returns the same SDP TA+TB as before, three of the messages can be skipped.

Receiving the original stream. Sometimes a user wants to receive both the original stream, for example audio, and the transcoded stream, for example the output of the speech-to-text conversion. One solution is to use the SDP group attribute with Flow Identification semantics, which allows a stream to be sent to two different transport addresses in parallel. The problem with that solution is that the majority of SIP user agents do not support Flow Identification, that only a small fraction of the few user agents that do support it also support sending simultaneous copies of the same media stream at the same time, and that Flow Identification forces both copies of the stream to use the same codec.

The memo therefore recommends that the transcoder, rather than a user agent, replicates the media stream. A transcoder receiving a session description with an audio stream for B, an audio stream for A marked as receive-only, and a text stream for A performs speech-to-text and text-to-speech conversions between the first audio stream and the text stream, and in addition copies the first audio stream to the second audio stream and sends it to A.
sections.plainLanguage: The caller can also be the one who brings the translator in, and then it gets to decide how many media streams the call has. A deaf user who wants to hear the original audio as well as read the text is better served if the translator makes the copy, because most phones cannot handle receiving one stream twice.

sections.title: Parallel and Series Transcoders
sections.content:
Transcoding services in parallel. Transcoding services sometimes consist of human relays, for example a person performing speech-to-text and text-to-speech conversions for a session. If the same person is involved in both conversions, that is from A to B and from B to A, they have access to all of the conversation. To provide some degree of privacy, two different people are sometimes allocated to do the job, one handling A to B and the other B to A. This disposition is also useful for automated transcoding services, where one machine converts text to synthetic speech and another performs voice recognition. The scenario involves four different sessions: A-T1, T1-B, B-T2 and T2-A. A invokes T1 and T2, and the flow has A invite each transcoder in turn, then send one combined INVITE to B describing both directions, and B answers with a single session description for both. Four media streams are then established: text from A to T1, audio from T1 to B, audio from B to T2, and text from T2 to A. The memo notes that B, the user agent server, needs to support two media streams, one sendonly and one recvonly, and that some user agents, although they support a single sendrecv media stream, do not support a different media line per direction. Implementers are encouraged to build support for this feature.

Multiple transcoding services in series. In a distributed environment, a complex transcoding service, for example English text to Spanish speech, is often provided by several servers. One server performs English text to Spanish text translation, and its output is fed into a server that performs text-to-speech conversion. The flow shows A invoking T1 and T2, with the chain running A to T1, T1 to T2, and T2 to B, and the session descriptions naming the pair of streams at each hop.
sections.plainLanguage: Two arrangements cover most needs. In parallel, two different translators handle the two directions, so neither sees the whole conversation. In series, the output of one translator is the input of the next, which is how a document gets translated and then turned into speech.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
RFC 3725 discusses the security considerations that relate to the use of third party call control in SIP, and those considerations apply here, because this document describes how to use 3pcc to invoke a transcoding service.

In particular, RFC 3725 states that end-to-end media security is based on the exchange of keying material within SDP and depends on the controller behaving properly: the controller should not try to disable the security mechanisms offered by the other parties. As a result it is trivially possible for the controller to insert itself as an intermediary on the media exchange if it should so desire. In this document the controller is the user agent invoking the transcoder, and there is a media session established using 3pcc between the remote user agent and the transcoder. The attack described in RFC 3725 therefore does not constitute a threat, because the controller is the user agent invoking the transcoding service and it has access to the media anyway by definition. It seems unlikely that a user agent would attempt to launch an attack against its own session by disabling security between the transcoder and the remote user agent.

Regarding end-to-end media security from the user agents' point of view, the transcoder needs access to the media in order to perform its function, so by definition the transcoder behaves as a man in the middle. User agents that do not want a particular transcoder to have access to all the media exchanged between them can use a different transcoder for each direction, and can also use different transcoders for different media types.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone who can see both ends of a call could stop the encryption. Here the party doing the signalling is the caller itself, and it already has the media, so there is nothing to steal by doing that. The real point is that the translator has to see the media unencrypted, so anyone worried about that should use a different translator for each direction.

data.title: SDP in the flow of Figure 1
data.code:
(1) INVITE SDP A

       m=audio 20000 RTP/AVP 0
       c=IN IP4 A.example.com

(2) INVITE SDP A+B

       m=audio 20000 RTP/AVP 0
       c=IN IP4 A.example.com
       m=text 40000 RTP/AVP 96
       c=IN IP4 B.example.com
       a=rtpmap:96 t140/1000

(3) 200 OK SDP TA+TB

       m=audio 30000 RTP/AVP 0
       c=IN IP4 T.example.com
       m=text 30002 RTP/AVP 96
       c=IN IP4 T.example.com
       a=rtpmap:96 t140/1000

(5) 200 OK SDP TA

       m=audio 30000 RTP/AVP 0
       c=IN IP4 T.example.com

messages.label: INVITE SDP A
messages.note: A proposes a session that consists of one audio stream.

messages.label: INVITE SDP A+B
messages.note: B wants to send and receive only text, so it invites a transcoder that will do both speech-to-text and text-to-speech conversions.

messages.label: 200 OK SDP TA+TB
messages.note: The transcoder answers with the addresses it will use to receive media from A and from B.

messages.label: 200 OK SDP TA
messages.note: The transcoder passes the answer back to A, with the addresses it will use for the audio stream.

messages.label: ACK
messages.note: A acknowledges, and the four media streams are established.

viz.caption: TWO TRANSCODERS IN PARALLEL AND TWO IN SERIES
